faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other such that, from Earth's viewpoint, one star periodically passes in front of the other. When this happens, the combined light we receive dips - we see a dip in brightness in the light curve. By studying the pattern, size, and timing of these dips, astronomers can measure the orbital period and learn about the stars' properties.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?

faqs.answer: 'Candidate' means a star showing eclipsing-binary-like patterns in its light curve that has not yet been checked for contamination from nearby stars. 'Confirmed' means the star has passed the automated pixel-level check, which verifies that the eclipse signal comes from the target star itself and not from a nearby object. Confirmation here means passing this site's vetting pipeline - it does not mean the system has been independently verified or studied by other astronomers.
faqs.question: What does 'candidate' vs 'confirmed' mean on this site?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter uses a machine learning model (hist_gradient_boosting) trained on 1649 labeled examples to assign a confidence score to each candidate. This score reflects how likely the candidate is a real eclipsing binary. The model performs better than the rule-based baseline method. However, this score is a second opinion only - it does not currently gate which candidates get checked or make any filtering decision in the pipeline.
faqs.question: What is the machine learning screening score?

faqs.answer: After statistical and novelty vetting, each candidate undergoes an automated pixel-level check. This computational test examines where in the image the brightness dip occurs, confirming that the eclipse signal originates from the target star and not from a nearby contaminant star. The check is fully automated and requires no human review.
faqs.question: How does the pixel-level check work?

faqs.answer: The pipeline uses an odd/even eclipse-depth test: it compares the depth of odd-numbered eclipses in the light curve against even-numbered eclipses. If these depths differ significantly, it suggests the measured period may be an alias - a harmonic or fraction of the true period. When this test flags a concern, that caveat is noted on the candidate's individual page.
faqs.question: What happens if the eclipse period looks aliased?

faqs.answer: Yes. Each confirmed candidate is listed with its TESS sector, target ID, orbital period, and relative eclipse depths - all measurable directly from the public TESS light curve data. You can download the light curve and inspect it yourself to confirm the eclipse pattern or perform your own follow-up analysis.
faqs.question: Can I verify a candidate result myself?

faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter is where this pipeline's work ends. The candidate is available for other astronomers to study, but this project itself does not conduct or coordinate follow-up observations, spectroscopy, or independent confirmation. Any further scientific work - such as measuring stellar masses, refining orbital elements, or publishing results - lies outside this vetting pipeline.
faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it appears on this site?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies and vets candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. The pipeline begins by sampling target stars and extracting their light curves - records of how brightness changes over time. Candidates that show the statistical signatures of eclipsing binaries are cross-checked against six established variable-star catalogs to flag novel objects. Each candidate then undergoes an automated pixel-level check to confirm the signal comes from the target star itself and not from nearby contaminants. A machine learning model trained on 1649 labeled examples provides a second opinion on which candidates are most likely real, beating the rule-based baseline method. So far, the pipeline has confirmed 167 eclipsing binary candidates from 1.3% of the TESS survey area. While each candidate is vetted for on-target signal and novelty, follow-up observations by other researchers may refine orbital properties, classify star types, or reveal additional caveats specific to individual systems.
